supports: Actor/possessor respect can concern the addressee or a third person; it is not simply second-person reference.
Kenjougo I honors the action's relevant target, including the source viewed from borrowing/receiving; it is not identical to physical direction of transfer.
Own-side third-person humble actions are ordinary; particular listener/third-party actions can also use kenjougo I under explicitly qualified relations.
Itasu, mairu, mousu and oru are kenjougo II in the identified functions: formal self/own-side presentation to the hearer, not automatically honoring a named destination.
O/go...itasu combines target respect with formal presentation, rather than being automatically invalid double keigo.
Desu/masu and (de)gozaimasu are teineigo; bikago is separate and does not necessarily honor a person.
Productive respectful and humble patterns have specific lexical restrictions. Goranninaru/oideninaru/oyasumininaru/omeshininaru are learned special formations.
Go...kudasaru and corresponding kudasai are legitimate patterns; blindly inserting shite can instead change who is honored.
Linked honorific predicates are distinguished from doubling the same word; conventional doubled forms also exist.
Inside/outside company situations alter reference choices; the school example explicitly qualifies a universal organizational-name prohibition.
supplementarySources.qualification: Use the stated contemporary normative scope and its own exceptions, not a universal social hierarchy, an exhaustive business-keigo course or a claim that forms prove sincere admiration.

supplementarySources.inspected: Complete returned article text recovered from the actual HTML after simplified extraction removed Japanese table entries and examples.
supplementarySources.supports: Special-verb mapping leads, intact ordinary polite conjugation table, direct go-chuui-kudasai and o/go construction examples.
supplementarySources.qualification: Do not adopt its linear three-level framing, lowest-speaker rule, all-other-verbs productivity, rare-use assertion for o-ni-naru or universal double-keigo descriptions. The vocabulary labels incorrectly call oru and meshiagaru ru-verbs, and the omie-ni-narimasu teacher example has a misleading seeing translation. Official guidance supplies the adopted analysis.

dictionaryQualification: Actual relevant senses were read. Prefix 御 has distinct ご/お entries; do not generalize imperial/archaic readings to every pattern. 待つ/俟つ uses waiting; 屆ける is an older character form of the delivered verb, not a different proposed reading. 案内 has あんない/あない; the chosen guiding use and original kana are retained. 書く is writing a name, not every drawing sense; 見せる is showing a ticket, not medical 診せる. Generic label entries do not establish the five-category technical taxonomy: the official guide supplies that analysis. Other local prompt readings/glosses are author-reviewed rather than individually dictionary-verified.
spellingScope: Keep the productive auxiliary endpoints なる/する in kana, visibly stated before answering. The dictionary's combined 成る/為る headword plus respectful auxiliary sense does not alone establish every marked spelling in these exact compounds. This is a checked writing scope, not a universal grammatical ban. Recognized 御, 為さる, 致す, 御座います, 下さい and the specifically supported auxiliary 頂く are accepted with their requested inflections. The receiving-request task visibly limits its auxiliary to kana/頂, because exact contextual 戴く support has not been established. No equal-frequency claim.

dispositions.note: Six complete-message interpretations vary third-person/direct address, delivery/borrowing and existence/copula. The official humble-I distinction is defined rather than redefining all humility. Ordinary ending morphology and actor/beneficiary recovery remain in their exact original owners.
Four stem/verbal-noun conversions with nonpast/past and direct/third-person contexts; specific lexical compatibility, not unrestricted derivation.

Two なさる conversions and three いらっしゃる conversions cover doing plus coming, past presence and negative going. Ongoing ていらっしゃる and further common special verbs are explained for recognition only; no new full-paradigm mastery claim.
Four humble-I formations plus four bare/combined いたす formations. The relevant action party need not be its physical destination; bare いたす is formal II, not automatically a named target's respect.
Four conversions distinguish existence/availability from nominal identification with affirmative, negative and past operations. Human existence is not taught as ordinary modern 先生がございます.
Four compact お/ご...ください conversions and two negative-potential receiving questions. Ordinary てください, bare requests, and favor-question polarity stay in their published owners.

dispositions.facet: Service viewpoint and own-side third parties
dispositions.note: Four scoped transfers contrast customer and own-side actions; the manager case prevents a first-person-only humility shortcut. These are ordinary customer-service scenes, not universal organization rules or free pragmatic production.

Possessor respect, beautifying prefixes, additional special verbs, linked/doubled honorifics and organizational exceptions are bounded recognition notes. Full business-keigo discourse, unrestricted stance choice, every lexical exception and exhaustive special-verb paradigms remain later work.
